sections.title: How to read this loop
sections.lede: Two interviews, back to back. **Priya is first**, so she sets the frame.

items: **Priya is first and owns the escalation queue.** Lead with S1 — it's her metric told back to her.
**Dan is a craft interviewer.** Governance answers that sound good but aren't specific won't survive.

sections.title: Knowledge Programs & Measurement
sections.lede: She owns the escalation queue. Every answer should end with **a partner being better off**.

items.label: Consolidated 40 runbooks, escalations down 38%
items.q: Tell me about building buy-in for a knowledge program.
items.note: Lead with this — it's the closest thing you have to **her** metric.

star.s: Support had **~40 runbooks** across three tools, no owner, and no agreed source of truth. On-call was escalating cases that were already documented — nobody could find the answer.
star.t: Consolidate them **without becoming the person every update routed through**.
star.a: I audited every runbook against **six months of ticket data** to find which ones were actually load-bearing, retired the rest, and gave each survivor **a named owner and a review-by date**. Then I trained two Specialists to maintain their own.
star.r: **Escalations dropped 38%** in the following quarter, and the library kept working after I moved to other projects — because the people who used it owned it.

beats.t: I didn't delete anything unilaterally — I **published the audit** and gave owners two weeks to object. Three did, and they were right.

punch.label: The line
punch.text: “**A library a team can't maintain isn't a program, it's a favor.**”

items.label: Health metrics, tiered
items.q: How would you measure whether a knowledge base is healthy?

beats.t: **First contact resolution** and **CSAT** — what leadership should judge the program on.
**Coverage against top ticket drivers**, **article age against review-by dates**, **time from launch to published**.
Which articles get opened and **still escalate**. That gap is where the content is wrong rather than missing.

punch.label: The filter
punch.text: “**If the number moved and nobody would do anything differently, I don't build it.**”

sections.title: Governance & Craft
sections.lede: A craft interviewer. Name the artifact, name the metric, name what changed.

items.label: Constrained the template, review rounds 5 → 2
items.q: Tell me about a governance framework you built.

star.s: Release notes were drafted in a freeform doc. Every version took **about five review rounds**, mostly arguing about structure rather than substance.
star.t: Raise consistency **without adding a reviewer nobody had time for**.
star.a: I rebuilt the template and **limited which sections contributors could edit**, so structure was enforced by the artifact instead of by a person.
star.r: Review rounds fell **from about five to two per version**, and the notes got more consistent across authors who had never coordinated.

punch.label: The thesis
punch.text: “**Governance that depends on people remembering the style guide fails. Governance built into the template holds.**”

items.q: What would your first 90 days look like?
items.note: Expect this. Rehearse it as three blocks with **a deliverable each**.

beats.d: Deliverable: a baseline and a ranked gap list.
items: Baseline **FCR, article age, and coverage against top ticket drivers**.
Sit with Specialists to find **where they go when the KB fails them** — that shadow system shows what's missing.
**I don't want to have restructured anything in month one.**
**An owner and a review-by date on every article** — a person, not a team.
A **launch-readiness gate**, plus a fast lane so the gate never becomes the reason people route around it.

beats.d: Deliverable: the program is legible from outside.
items: **One metric visibly moving**, and a monthly written update already in rhythm.

punch.label: The close
punch.text: “The real signal is **being pulled into launch planning early instead of finding out at release**.”
